title: Force and torque conditions for equilibrium

learning_outcomes.text: understand that, when there is no resultant force and no resultant torque, a system is in equilibrium

prior_knowledge_summary: A moment measures the turning effect of a force about a point.
The formula to remember is M = Fd_perpendicular, where d_perpendicular is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
For a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about a point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point.
Choosing a pivot through an unknown force removes that force from a moment equation.
new_learning: Complete equilibrium requires zero resultant force and zero resultant torque at the same time.
Force balance and moment balance are separate checks and neither one alone proves equilibrium.
For coplanar forces, force balance can be applied independently in perpendicular directions before or after a moment equation is used.
not_yet_taught: Representing three equilibrium forces as a closed head-to-tail vector triangle.

visual_planning.reason: Six planned visuals separate translation from rotation, model the two-check method, support two worked systems, and correct the false idea that being still is enough for equilibrium. No assets were created in this text-package task.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: A shelf that does not fall but still turns
content: Imagine a light shelf floating with one 10 N upward force and one 10 N downward force. The forces are equal and opposite, so their vector sum is zero. Is the shelf definitely in equilibrium?

If the upward force acts near the left end and the downward force acts near the right end, the two forces turn the shelf in the same sense. Its centre does not accelerate, but the shelf begins to rotate. Zero resultant force has passed one test and failed to guarantee the whole result.
Equilibrium needs two independent promises: no linear acceleration and no angular acceleration. We will learn how to test both.

figure.purpose: Create the contradiction that equal and opposite forces can still rotate a body
figure.brief: Draw a light horizontal shelf with a 10 N upward force near its left end and a 10 N downward force near its right end. Show a curved clockwise rotation arrow but no translational arrow. Add the short question zero force, but equilibrium? Do not state the answer.
figure.alt_text: A shelf has equal opposite forces at different positions and a clockwise turning arrow.

blocks.title: Equilibrium has a force test and a torque test
content: The force test asks whether all forces add as vectors to zero. In a flat problem, this means the horizontal components sum to zero and the vertical components sum to zero. Passing this test means no linear acceleration.
The torque test asks whether the clockwise and anticlockwise turning effects cancel. Equivalently, the resultant torque about any point is zero. Passing this test means no angular acceleration.
A system is in equilibrium only when it passes both tests. It may be stationary, or it may move with constant velocity, because equilibrium describes zero acceleration rather than zero speed.

figure.purpose: Separate the translational and rotational conditions without merging their meanings
figure.brief: Create a two-column teacher sketch. Left column: force check, horizontal sum zero, vertical sum zero, no linear acceleration. Right column: torque check, clockwise sum equals anticlockwise sum, no angular acceleration. Join both columns to one highlighted box labelled equilibrium.
figure.alt_text: Two columns show that zero resultant force and zero resultant torque are both required for equilibrium.

blocks.title: Why one successful check is not enough
content: The opening shelf has zero resultant force because the 10 N forces cancel. Yet their lines of action are separated, so both moments act clockwise. The shelf has a non-zero resultant torque and is not in equilibrium.

The reverse failure is also possible. Push a box horizontally through its centre with 8 N while friction is only 3 N in the opposite direction. About the centre, neither force has a turning effect, so the resultant torque is zero. The 5 N resultant force still accelerates the box.
These examples give a reliable habit: never infer the force condition from the moment condition, and never infer the moment condition from the force condition. Write and check each one.

figure.purpose: Compare the two distinct ways a body can fail equilibrium
figure.brief: Draw two compact panels. Panel A shows equal opposite forces at separated lines of action, labelled resultant force zero and torque not zero. Panel B shows an 8 N push and 3 N friction through a box centre, labelled torque zero and resultant force 5 N. Use different colour coding for translation and rotation.
figure.alt_text: One panel fails only the torque test and another fails only the force test.

blocks.title: A hanging sign: use moments, then forces
content: A 1.20 m uniform sign arm is hinged at its left end. Its 90 N weight acts at the midpoint. A vertical cable at the right end holds it horizontal. The formula to remember is M = Fd_perpendicular. Here M is moment in N m, F is force in N and d_perpendicular is perpendicular distance in m.

Choose the hinge as pivot. The hinge force then has zero distance from the pivot. The weight gives a clockwise moment 90 x 0.60 = 54 N m. Let the vertical cable force be T. Its anticlockwise moment is T x 1.20. Rotational balance gives T x 1.20 = 54, so T = 45 N.

That only passes the torque test. Now apply vertical force balance. If the vertical hinge force is H, upward forces equal downward forces: H + 45 = 90, so H = 45 N upward. Horizontal balance is already satisfied because no horizontal force acts in this simplified system.

Independent check: take moments about the right end. The 45 N hinge force acts 1.20 m away and the 90 N weight acts 0.60 m away. Their moments are both 54 N m in opposite senses, so the result is consistent.

figure.purpose: Model the sequence of choosing a pivot, balancing moments, then balancing forces
figure.brief: Draw a horizontal 1.20 m sign arm hinged at the left, with 90 N downward at its midpoint, vertical cable T upward at the right, and hinge reaction H upward. Beside it show three short numbered lines: pivot at hinge, T x 1.20 = 90 x 0.60, H + T = 90. Keep the final values visible because this is a teaching figure.
figure.alt_text: A hinged sign arm is solved first by moment balance and then by vertical force balance.

blocks.title: An angled cable: resolve before balancing
content: Now a 0.80 m beam is hinged to a wall and supported at its free end by a 50 N cable at 30 degrees above the horizontal. The cable has horizontal component 50 cos 30 degrees = 43.3 N and vertical component 50 sin 30 degrees = 25.0 N.

Only the vertical cable component has a moment about the hinge because the horizontal component acts along the beam through the pivot. The anticlockwise moment is 25.0 x 0.80 = 20.0 N m. If a load W hangs 0.50 m from the hinge, rotational balance gives W x 0.50 = 20.0, so W = 40.0 N.

Next use force balance. Horizontally, the hinge force must be 43.3 N to the right to balance the cable component to the left. Vertically, let upward be positive: H_y + 25.0 - 40.0 = 0, so H_y = 15.0 N upward.

Check the physical story. The cable supplies some upward support, but not enough to equal the load by itself, so an upward hinge component is reasonable. The horizontal cable pull must also be balanced even though it produced no moment about the chosen pivot.

figure.purpose: Show that a force component can vanish from one moment equation but remain essential to force balance
figure.brief: Draw a 0.80 m horizontal beam hinged at a wall, a 50 N cable at 30 degrees above the beam attached at the free end, and a 40 N load 0.50 m from the hinge. Resolve the cable into 43.3 N horizontal and 25.0 N vertical components. Add separate small boxes for moment balance and x/y force balance.
figure.alt_text: An angled cable is resolved before moments and horizontal and vertical force balances are applied.

blocks.title: Still for one instant does not mean equilibrium
content: It feels reasonable to call any motionless object balanced because everyday objects that remain still are often in equilibrium. The missing word is remain.

A tossed ball has zero speed for one instant at the top of its path, but its weight still acts downward. The resultant force is not zero, so the ball accelerates and is not in equilibrium. A compressed spring block can also be momentarily still while a non-zero spring force sends it back.

Ask about forces and torques, not just the speed shown in one snapshot. Constant velocity gives zero acceleration and therefore zero resultant force. Instantaneous zero speed alone tells us nothing about the resultant force.

figure.purpose: Correct the snapshot-based misconception about rest and equilibrium
figure.brief: Create a comparison sketch. Left: a book remaining still on a table with balanced normal force and weight. Right: a ball at the top of a toss with v = 0 at that instant and one downward weight arrow, plus a small downward acceleration arrow. Label both snapshots still now? and highlight only the book as equilibrium.
figure.alt_text: A stationary book is in equilibrium, while a momentarily stationary tossed ball is not.

blocks.title: The two-check equilibrium routine
content: First identify every external force and resolve any angled force into useful components. Choose positive directions and keep the signs consistent.

Second choose a pivot that removes difficult unknown forces. Apply the principle from the previous lesson: for a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about a point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point.
Third return to translation. Apply zero resultant force independently in the horizontal and vertical directions. A force that vanished from the moment equation may still be needed here.

Finally perform a separate check. You can take moments about another point, add all force components explicitly, inspect units, or ask whether each calculated direction makes physical sense. Do not use a closed vector triangle yet. That representation belongs to the next lesson.

concepts_taught: complete equilibrium requires zero resultant force and zero resultant torque
force balance and moment balance are independent conditions
equilibrium may be static or dynamic because it requires zero acceleration, not zero speed
misconceptions_addressed: zero resultant force alone proves equilibrium
zero resultant torque alone proves equilibrium
an object with zero speed at one instant must be in equilibrium
a force that has zero moment about the chosen pivot can be ignored completely
skills_students_can_now_use: state and test both conditions for equilibrium
